---
title: "Performance Profiling and Bottleneck Identification"
---

## Purpose {.unnumbered}

_Why does optimizing an operator without measuring its arithmetic intensity almost always waste engineering effort?_

In machine learning systems engineering, optimizing code based on intuition is a recipe for wasted effort: accelerating a matrix multiplication that accounts for only 2% of runtime or vectorizing an operator that is strictly memory bandwidth-bound produces zero observable speedup. To make disciplined, high-impact performance optimizations, systems engineers rely on empirical measurement frameworks. Every deep learning operation is physically constrained by one of two hardware ceilings: **Memory Bandwidth** (the rate at which bytes can be transferred from RAM/HBM to compute registers) or **Compute Throughput** (the rate at which ALUs and Tensor Cores can execute arithmetic instructions). By formulating exact parameter counts, theoretical FLOP calculations, memory allocation tracking, and latency profiling into a unified **Roofline Model**, we provide the diagnostic foundation that guides all subsequent compression and acceleration techniques in TinyTorch.

::: {.callout-learning-objectives}
## Learning Objectives

- **Construct** the `Profiler` engine in TinyTorch, measuring parameter counts, theoretical FLOPs, peak memory allocation, and latency percentiles.
- **Derive** closed-form FLOP equations for Linear projections, Conv2d filters, and Multi-Head Attention blocks.
- **Formulate** the Williams Roofline Model and compute the **Arithmetic Intensity** ($I = \text{FLOPs} / \text{Byte}$) for foundational operators.
- **Execute** statistically rigorous latency profiling with warm-up cycles, garbage collection isolation, and percentile reporting (P50, P90, P99).
- **Diagnose** whether a bottleneck requires memory reduction (quantization, fusion) or arithmetic acceleration (tiling, vectorization).
:::

## The First Principle of ML Systems: Measure First

Before modifying a single line of kernel code, we must profile the baseline workload across four fundamental systems dimensions:

```
┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│  The Four Pillars of ML Performance Profiling               │
├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
│  1. Parameters (P) : Storage footprint & static weight RAM  │
│  2. FLOPs (F)      : Total floating-point arithmetic volume │
│  3. Memory (M)     : Dynamic activation peak buffer size    │
│  4. Latency (T)    : Wall-clock execution time & percentiles│
└─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
```

---

## Parameter Counting and Theoretical FLOP Formulations

A **FLOP (Floating-Point Operation)** represents a single arithmetic operation (one addition or one multiplication). A fused multiply-accumulate ($y \leftarrow y + a \times b$) counts as **2 FLOPs**.

### Dense Linear Layer

For $\mathbf{Y} = \mathbf{X} \mathbf{W} + \mathbf{b}$ with $\mathbf{X} \in \mathbb{R}^{B \times D_{\text{in}}}$ and $\mathbf{W} \in \mathbb{R}^{D_{\text{in}} \times D_{\text{out}}}$:

$$\text{Parameters} = D_{\text{in}} \times D_{\text{out}} + D_{\text{out}}$$

$$\text{FLOPs} = 2 \times B \times D_{\text{in}} \times D_{\text{out}}$$

### 2D Convolutional Layer

For input $(B, C_{\text{in}}, H_{\text{in}}, W_{\text{in}})$ and filters $(C_{\text{out}}, C_{\text{in}}, K_h, K_w)$:

$$\text{Parameters} = C_{\text{out}} \times C_{\text{in}} \times K_h \times K_w + C_{\text{out}}$$

$$\text{FLOPs} = 2 \times B \times C_{\text{out}} \times H_{\text{out}} \times W_{\text{out}} \times (C_{\text{in}} \cdot K_h \cdot K_w)$$

### Multi-Head Self-Attention Block

For sequence length $S$, model dimension $D$, and $H$ heads ($d_k = D/H$):

- Q, K, V, O Linear Projections ($4 \times \text{Linear}$): $4 \times (2 B S D^2) = 8 B S D^2\text{ FLOPs}$.
- Attention Logits ($\mathbf{Q} \mathbf{K}^T$): $2 B H S^2 d_k = 2 B S^2 D\text{ FLOPs}$.
- Value Aggregation ($\text{Softmax} \times \mathbf{V}$): $2 B H S^2 d_k = 2 B S^2 D\text{ FLOPs}$.

$$\text{Total Attention FLOPs} = 8 B S D^2 + 4 B S^2 D$$

---

## The Williams Roofline Model

The **Roofline Model** (Williams et al., 2009) defines the maximum achievable performance of any hardware system as a function of **Arithmetic Intensity ($I$)**:

$$\text{Arithmetic Intensity } I = \frac{\text{Total Arithmetic FLOPs}}{\text{Total DRAM / HBM Bytes Transferred}} \quad \left( \frac{\text{FLOPs}}{\text{Byte}} \right)$$

$$\text{Attainable Performance } P = \min\left( \text{Peak Compute Throughput } P_{\text{peak}}, \quad I \times \text{Peak Memory Bandwidth } BW_{\text{peak}} \right)$$

The intersection point where compute and memory limits meet is the **Ridge Point** ($I_{\text{ridge}}$):

$$I_{\text{ridge}} = \frac{P_{\text{peak}}\text{ (FLOP/s)}}{BW_{\text{peak}}\text{ (Bytes/s)}}$$

::: {#fig-roofline-model}
![](../quarto/assets/images/diagrams/14_profiling-diag-1.svg)

**Figure 14.1: The Roofline Performance Model.** Operators with arithmetic intensity below the ridge point (such as LayerNorm, ReLU, and single-token generation) are memory-bound. Batched GEMMs and large convolutions operate in the compute-bound plateau.
:::

On modern accelerator hardware, the ridge point is exceptionally high. For example, an NVIDIA H100 SXM5 GPU delivers $\sim 1{,}000\text{ TFLOPS}$ ($10^{15}\text{ FLOP/s}$) of FP16 Tensor Core compute against $3.35\text{ TB/s}$ of High-Bandwidth Memory (HBM3) bandwidth,[^hbm3-footnote] resulting in a ridge point:

$$I_{\text{ridge}} = \frac{1{,}000 \times 10^{12}\text{ FLOP/s}}{3.35 \times 10^{12}\text{ Bytes/s}} \approx 298.5\text{ FLOPs/Byte}$$

By contrast, on-chip SRAM caches located directly within each Streaming Multiprocessor (SM) deliver over $100\text{ TB/s}$ of aggregate bandwidth at sub-nanosecond latency,[^sram-footnote] demonstrating why keeping intermediate data pinned in registers and L1/SRAM is the central imperative of kernel optimization.

[^hbm3-footnote]: High-Bandwidth Memory (HBM3/HBM3e) achieves multi-terabyte-per-second bandwidth (e.g., 3.35 TB/s on NVIDIA H100 SXM5, 4.8 TB/s on H200, and 8.0 TB/s on Blackwell B200) by vertically stacking DRAM dies with through-silicon vias (TSVs) over an ultra-wide 5120-bit interface, compared to standard dual-channel DDR5 server memory at ~50–100 GB/s across a 128-bit bus.

[^sram-footnote]: Modern GPU Streaming Multiprocessors (SMs) allocate 128 KB to 228 KB of ultra-fast on-chip SRAM configurable as L1 data cache and shared memory. Across 132 SMs on an H100 GPU, this represents ~30 MB of aggregate on-chip SRAM delivering over 100 TB/s of bandwidth with ~1–2 ns latency, compared to off-chip HBM3 access at 3.35 TB/s and ~50–100 ns latency.

::: {.callout-principle}
## The Diagnostic Rule

- **If $I < I_{\text{ridge}}$ (Memory-Bound)**: Arithmetic pipelines spend the majority of clock cycles stalled waiting for data transfers over the memory bus. Optimizing arithmetic instructions (e.g., vectorization) will yield **zero speedup**. You must reduce memory traffic via **Operator Fusion** (Chapter 17) or **Quantization** (Chapter 15).
- **If $I > I_{\text{ridge}}$ (Compute-Bound)**: Memory transfers are completely hidden behind compute latency; you must maximize arithmetic throughput via **Cache Tiling** and **Systolic Matrix Multiplication** (Chapter 17).
:::

---

## Latency Profiling: Warmups and Percentiles

Measuring execution time in modern operating systems is fraught with noise from CPU frequency scaling, thread context switching, and background garbage collection.

A production-grade profiling protocol enforces three invariants:

1. **Warmup Cycles**: Run 5–10 iterations before measurement to populate CPU L1/L2 caches and stabilize processor clock governors.
2. **Garbage Collection Isolation**: Disable automatic Python garbage collection (`gc.disable()`) during timed loops to prevent spurious latency spikes.
3. **Statistical Percentiles**: In real-time inference, reporting only mean latency hides long-tail tail latency. Frameworks report **P50 (Median)**, **P90**, and **P99 (Worst 1%)** latency.

---

## Implementing the Profiler in TinyTorch

```python
# Listing 14.1: The Profiler Engine in TinyTorch
import time
import tracemalloc
import gc
from typing import Dict, Any, List
import numpy as np

class Profiler:
    """
    Comprehensive ML systems profiler for parameters, memory, FLOPs, and latency.
    """

    def __init__(self) -> None:
        self.results: Dict[str, Any] = {}

    def count_parameters(self, model: Any) -> Dict[str, int]:
        """Count total and trainable parameters in model."""
        total_params = 0
        trainable_params = 0

        for p in model.parameters():
            num_elem = p.data.size
            total_params += num_elem
            if p.requires_grad:
                trainable_params += num_elem

        return {
            'total_parameters': total_params,
            'trainable_parameters': trainable_params,
            'memory_bytes': total_params * 4,
            'memory_mb': (total_params * 4) / (1024 * 1024)
        }

    def benchmark_latency(
        self,
        func: Any,
        *args: Any,
        warmup: int = 5,
        runs: int = 50
    ) -> Dict[str, float]:
        """
        Measure execution latency percentiles with warmup and GC isolation.
        """
        # 1. Warmup cycles to populate caches
        for _ in range(warmup):
            func(*args)

        latencies = []
        gc_was_enabled = gc.isenabled()
        gc.disable()

        try:
            for _ in range(runs):
                t0 = time.perf_counter()
                func(*args)
                t1 = time.perf_counter()
                latencies.append((t1 - t0) * 1000.0)  # Milliseconds
        finally:
            if gc_was_enabled:
                gc.enable()

        latencies_sorted = np.sort(latencies)
        return {
            'mean_ms': float(np.mean(latencies)),
            'std_ms': float(np.std(latencies)),
            'p50_ms': float(np.percentile(latencies_sorted, 50)),
            'p90_ms': float(np.percentile(latencies_sorted, 90)),
            'p99_ms': float(np.percentile(latencies_sorted, 99))
        }

    def measure_peak_memory(self, func: Any, *args: Any) -> float:
        """Measure peak dynamic memory allocated during execution (MB)."""
        tracemalloc.start()
        func(*args)
        current, peak = tracemalloc.get_traced_memory()
        tracemalloc.stop()
        return peak / (1024.0 * 1024.0)
```

## Profiling a Transformer in TinyTorch

```python
# Listing 14.2: Profiling TinyGPT Performance
from tinytorch.core.transformers import GPT

gpt = GPT(vocab_size=1000, max_seq_len=128, d_model=128, num_heads=4, num_layers=4)
profiler = Profiler()

# 1. Profile parameters
param_stats = profiler.count_parameters(gpt)
print(f"Total Parameters: {param_stats['total_parameters']:,} ({param_stats['memory_mb']:.2f} MB)")

# 2. Profile latency on batch of shape (4, 64)
dummy_input = Tensor(np.random.randint(0, 1000, size=(4, 64), dtype=np.int32))
latency_stats = profiler.benchmark_latency(gpt, dummy_input)
print(f"Forward Latency: P50 = {latency_stats['p50_ms']:.2f} ms | P99 = {latency_stats['p99_ms']:.2f} ms")

# 3. Peak memory
peak_mem = profiler.measure_peak_memory(gpt, dummy_input)
print(f"Peak Dynamic Memory Allocation: {peak_mem:.2f} MB")
```

::: {.callout-note}
## PyTorch Systems Bridge: `torch.profiler` and Graph-Level Cost Models

In production PyTorch pipelines, performance diagnostics are performed via `torch.profiler` and the Kineto tracing engine:

```python
import torch
from torch.profiler import profile, record_function, ProfilerActivity

with profile(
    activities=[ProfilerActivity.CPU, ProfilerActivity.CUDA],
    record_shapes=True,
    profile_memory=True,
    with_flops=True
) as prof:
    with record_function("model_inference"):
        model(inputs)

# Export visual timeline trace for Chrome / Perfetto inspection
prof.export_chrome_trace("timeline_trace.json")
print(prof.key_averages().table(sort_by="cuda_time_total", row_limit=10))
```

Under the hood, modern compilers like **PyTorch 2.0 `torch.compile` (TorchInductor)** evaluate the Roofline arithmetic intensity of captured FX graph subgraphs. When an operator chain has low arithmetic intensity ($I < I_{\text{ridge}}$), TorchInductor automatically fuses the sequence into a unified OpenAI Triton GPU kernel, eliminating intermediate HBM reads and writes.
:::

## Summary

In this chapter, we constructed the diagnostic profiling engine of TinyTorch. We examined why performance optimization must be grounded in empirical data, deriving exact mathematical formulas for parameter storage and theoretical FLOP counts.

We formulated the Williams Roofline Model, defining the critical boundary between memory-bound and compute-bound operators using Arithmetic Intensity. We implemented the complete `Profiler` engine with latency percentiles and memory allocation tracking, equipping ourselves with the measurement tools required to guide the systems optimizations in the upcoming chapters.

::: {.callout-takeaways}
## Chapter Takeaways

- **The Roofline Principle**: Operators are either bounded by DRAM/HBM memory bandwidth or ALU compute throughput; arithmetic intensity ($I = \text{FLOPs}/\text{Byte}$) identifies the bottleneck.
- **FLOP Accounting**: Standard Linear projections execute $2 B D_{\text{in}} D_{\text{out}}$ FLOPs; Multi-Head Attention executes $8 B S D^2 + 4 B S^2 D$ FLOPs.
- **Latency Rigor**: Reliable benchmarking requires cache warmup passes, disabling Python garbage collection during timed runs, and reporting percentile metrics (P50, P90, P99).
- **Targeted Optimization**: Memory-bound operators require memory traffic reduction (quantization, fusion); compute-bound operators require hardware parallelism and cache tiling.
:::

::: {.callout-chapter-connection}
## Chapter Connection: Shrinking Models with Low Precision

How do we reduce memory traffic by 4× without retraining our models from scratch?
